{{Short description|Austrian-born American mathematician (1924–2024)}}
'''(Ilse) Lisl Novak Gaal''' (January 17, 1924 – October 7, 2024)<ref name=wbm /> was an Austrian-born American mathematician known for her contributions to [[set theory]] and [[Galois theory]].{{r|julia}} She was the first woman to hold a [[tenure-track]] position in mathematics at [[Cornell University]],{{r|wmfc}} and was an associate professor emeritus at the [[University of Minnesota]].<ref>{{cite book |title=American Men & Women of Science: G-I |date=2003 |publisher=R.R. Bowker |edition=Volume 3}}</ref> Gaal died in 2024, at the age of 100.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lisl Gaal |url=https://cse.umn.edu/math/lisl-gaal |website=University of Minnesota College of Science and Engineering |access-date=17 December 2024}}</ref>

==Contributions==
Gaal's dissertation work was in the [[foundations of mathematics]]. It proved that two different systems for [[set theory]] that had previously been proposed as foundational were [[Equiconsistency|equiconsistent]]: either both are valid or both lead to contradictions. These two systems were [[Zermelo set theory]] and [[Von Neumann–Bernays–Gödel set theory|Von Neumann set theory]]. They differed from each other in that von Neumann had added to Zermelo's theory a notion of [[Class (set theory)|classes]], collections of mathematical objects that are defined by some property but do not necessarily form a set. (Often, intuitively, proper classes are "too big" to form sets; for instance, the collection of all sets cannot itself be a set, by [[Russell's paradox]], but it can be a class.) Gaal's work showed that introducing this extra notion of a class is a safe step, one that does not introduce any new inconsistencies into the system.{{r|julia}}

Gaal was also the author of two books:
*''Classical Galois Theory with Examples'' (Markham Publishing, 1971; third ed., Chelsea Publishing, 1979; reprinted 1998){{r|cgt}}
*''A Mathematical Gallery'' (American Mathematical Society, 2017){{r|amg}}

==Early life and education==
Gaal was born in [[Vienna]] on January 17, 1924,{{r|wbm}} the daughter of a gynecologist and the sister of [[Gertrude M. Novak]], who became a physician in Chicago. She and her two sisters escaped Nazi Germany, and moved with their family to [[New York City]].{{r|gertrude}}

After graduating from [[Hunter College]] with an A.B. in 1944,{{r|wbm}} Gaal earned a doctorate in 1948 from [[Harvard University]], through [[Radcliffe College]]. Her dissertation, ''On the Consistency of Goedel's Axioms for Class and Set Theory Relative to a Weaker Set of Axioms'', was jointly supervised by [[Lynn Harold Loomis]] and [[Willard Van Orman Quine]].{{r|julia|wmfc|mgp}}

==Later career==
Gaal lived in [[Berkeley, California]] from 1950 to 1951.{{r|julia}} She and her husband, mathematician [[Steven Gaal]], both moved to [[Cornell University]], beginning as instructors in 1953 but then in 1954 being promoted to assistant professors. This step was the first time the Cornell mathematics department had offered a tenure-track position to a woman. She also became the first woman at Cornell to advise the doctorate of a mathematics student, Angelo Margaris.{{r|wmfc}}

The Gaals moved again in 1957, to the [[University of Minnesota]],{{r|wmfc}} where she became an associate professor emeritus.{{r|julia}}

In later life, Gaal became a [[Lithography|lithographer]], making prints that combined mathematical themes with Minnesota scenes.{{r|mix|pap}}
Her book ''A Mathematical Gallery'' collects some of her mathematical illustrations.{{r|amg}}
